1254.title: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
1254.hook: a child's landscape often starts with one line across the page. the hymn's fifth verse stretches a line too, and then asks about it
1254.carry: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
1254.tomorrow: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
1254.howItsDone: The fifth verse of the Nasadiya Sukta is read in more than one way by Hindu commentators and modern readers, and the hymn as a whole is kept in Vedic recitation learned from a teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nasadiya Sukta's fourth verse: kama, desire, the first seed of mind, and poets searching their hearts for the bond of what is in what is not.

Hand a child a blank sheet and a crayon and ask for a landscape. Sometimes the first mark is a line straight across the page: the ground. With that one stroke, the page has an up and a down. Sky goes above the line; grass and roots go below. Before the line, the paper was just white. After it, there are places to put things. The Nasadiya Sukta's fifth verse draws a line too. But as soon as it's down, the verse starts asking questions about it.
screen: `A BLANK SHEET, A CRAYON.` → `ONE LINE ACROSS: THE GROUND.` → `NOW THERE'S AN UP AND A DOWN.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, the verse says: their cord was stretched across. Was there something below it? Was there something above it? Then: there were seed-placers, there were great powers. Their own power below, a giving forth above. The word for cord is rashmi. It can mean a ray of light, a rein, a line. Stretched across, it does what the child's crayon does: it makes a below and an above. This verse is hard, and honesty about that is part of reading it. The hymn doesn't say whose cord it is. Some readers take their to mean the poets of the verse before, the ones who searched their hearts, as if their insight drew the line between what is and what is not. Others read it differently, and the hymn leaves the question standing. Even while it describes, the verse keeps asking. A plainer hymn might simply say: earth below, heaven above. This one puts a question mark on each side of its own line. Then the second half: seed-placers, great powers, and a pair. Their own power below, something that holds and carries. A giving forth above, something that moves outward. One reading hears two halves of a whole, a receiving and a giving, needing each other. On an ordinary day that picture can be small and close: a floor that holds a body, a breath that goes out from it.

segments.voice: Feel where you meet the chair or the floor; that's your line, and below it, let yourself be held, the weight going down, nothing for you to do. Above it, notice the breath moving out and in, the part of you that gives forth, and stay with both at once, coming back to the line when you drift; if you pray, you can rest there in prayer.
The Nasadiya Sukta. The hymn of creation. In its fifth verse, a cord stretched across, a below and an above, and a question asked about each.

1255.title: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
1255.hook: "where was I before I was born?" the hymn's last two verses ask that question about everything, and end with "or perhaps"
1255.carry: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
1255.howItsDone: Hindu commentators and modern readers interpret the Nasadiya Sukta's closing 'or perhaps does not know' in different ways, and the hymn is still kept in traditional Vedic recitation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nasadiya Sukta's fifth verse: a cord stretched across, and a question asked on each side of it.

Where was I before I was born? A small child might ask it at bedtime, wide awake, while the grown-up in the doorway searches for an answer. There are a few ways to handle it. Give a confident answer. Change the subject. Or sit on the edge of the bed and say, honestly, that's a big one, and nobody has seen all the way back. The Nasadiya Sukta has circled a bigger version of that question since its first verse. In its last two, it asks it straight out.
screen: `WHERE WAS I BEFORE I WAS BORN?` → `A CONFIDENT ANSWER, OR A NEW SUBJECT?` → `OR: NOBODY HAS SEEN THAT FAR BACK.`

segments.voice: Verse six opens with a question. Ko addha veda. Who really knows? Who here could declare it, where this was born, where this creation came from? Then a startling line. The gods, it says, came after this world's making. They are on this side of it. So even the gods weren't there to see the start. Who, then, knows where it arose? Verse seven tries one more answer. This creation, wherever it came from, whether it was made or whether it wasn't, the one who watches over it in the highest heaven surely knows. And then the hymn's last words: or perhaps that one does not know. In Sanskrit, so anga veda yadi va na veda. Readers have heard that ending more than one way. Some traditional readers take it as honoring the overseer: the beginning is so deep that only the highest one could know it, if anyone can. Some modern readers hear plain, honest doubt, kept inside scripture. Others hear both at once, a reverence that refuses to pretend. The hymn simply stops, with no verse to tidy things up. It ends where a wise grown-up at a bedside might: that's a big one, and here is how far anyone has seen. The question stays open, and the hymn is still sung.
screen: `KO ADDHA VEDA: WHO REALLY KNOWS?` · `THE GODS CAME AFTER THE MAKING.` · `THE ONE IN HIGHEST HEAVEN SURELY KNOWS.` · `OR PERHAPS DOES NOT KNOW.`

segments.voice: Bring up one thing you know because you were there, a face, a kitchen, a street you walked, and silently call it seen; then something you only believe, or were told, or guess at, and call it not seen, gently, with no judgment. Go back and forth for a while, noticing that both can be held in the same quiet mind; if you pray, you can offer the not-seen to God.
The Nasadiya Sukta. The hymn of creation. It ends: the one in highest heaven surely knows, or perhaps that one does not know.

1256.title: the Purusha Sukta
1256.hook: a festival crowd seen from above is all heads, hands and feet. the Purusha Sukta opens with a person like that, and bigger than the world
1256.howItsDone: The Purusha Sukta is a hymn of the Rig Veda that Hindus recite in worship and in traditional Vedic chanting, and teachers of different schools quote and interpret it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nasadiya Sukta ended: the one in highest heaven surely knows, or perhaps does not know.

A festival crowd, photographed from a rooftop. At first it looks like one moving surface. Then you zoom in. Heads, thousands of them. Hands in the air. Sandals, a child on someone's shoulders. One crowd, and countless people, and you can't quite say where one ends and the next begins. The Rig Veda has a hymn that opens on a picture like that, except the crowd is one person, and the person is bigger than the world. After a hymn that asked who knows, here's one that begins by describing.
screen: `A CROWD FROM A ROOFTOP.` → `ONE THING, COUNTLESS PEOPLE.` → `NOW MAKE IT ONE PERSON.`

segments.voice: Purusha means person, a man, a human being. Earlier on this path the word meant the quiet seer in the Yoga Sutras. Here, in the Rig Veda, it names a cosmic person. The hymn opens: sahasra-shirsha purushah. The Purusha has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet. Some readers hear thousand as a way of saying beyond counting: every head is in some sense his, every pair of eyes, every step. Then he covered the earth on every side, and stood beyond it by ten fingers' width. That small measure is strange and lovely. Not a mountain or an ocean: ten fingers. As if to say, he holds the whole world, and there's still a little more of him past its edge. Verse two widens it. Purusha eva idam sarvam. The Purusha is all this, whatever has been and whatever is to be. Past and future, in one person. Together the two verses have a double edge. The Purusha is everything there is, and also more than everything there is: inside the world, and just past its rim. Teachers of different Hindu schools read this person in their own ways. For today, stay with the opening picture: every face in that rooftop crowd, and a little beyond.
screen: `PURUSHA: A PERSON.` · `A THOUSAND HEADS, EYES AND FEET.` · `BEYOND THE EARTH BY TEN FINGERS.` · `ALL THIS, WHAT HAS BEEN AND WILL BE.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap and feel them from the inside: warmth, weight, a faint tingle. Then let your attention go to the air just past your fingertips, a few inches out, the room continuing, and rest there, the body and a little more; when you wander, come back to the fingertips. If you pray, you can rest in prayer there.
The Purusha Sukta. The hymn of the cosmic person: a thousand heads, eyes and feet, all that has been and will be, and still ten fingers more.

1257.title: the Purusha Sukta
1257.hook: a coworker you've known for years sings at a wedding, and you realize you've only met a part of them. the hymn says all beings are one quarter of the Purusha
1257.howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers cite the Purusha Sukta's 'a quarter of him is all beings' when speaking of the divine as present in the world and also beyond it, and the hymn is recited in Vedic chanting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Purusha Sukta opened: a person with a thousand heads, covering the earth and standing beyond it by ten fingers' width.
screen: `A THOUSAND HEADS, AND TEN FINGERS MORE.`

segments.voice: Someone you've worked beside for years, the one who fixes the printer and remembers birthdays, stands up at a wedding and sings. The room goes quiet, because the voice is extraordinary. You had no idea. You knew a real part of this person, nothing fake about it. But it was a part, and not the larger one. The Purusha Sukta's third verse does something like that with the whole world. It takes everything that exists, every star and ant and city, and says: this is the part of him you've met.
screen: `THE COWORKER WHO FIXES THE PRINTER.` → `THEN SHE SINGS.` → `YOU'D ONLY MET A PART.`

segments.voice: Verse three: such is his greatness, and the Purusha is greater still. The thousand heads, the earth covered on every side: all of it is his greatness, and he is more. Then a proportion. Pado asya vishva bhutani. A quarter of him is all beings. Pada means a foot, and it can also mean a quarter. All beings, everything that lives and dies, are one quarter. Three quarters of him, the verse says, are immortal, in heaven. Verse four goes on. With three quarters the Purusha rose up. The one quarter came to be here, again and again, and from it he spread out in every direction, into what eats and what doesn't eat: the hungry sparrow and the stone. So the world, for all its size, is the smaller share. On the hymn's picture, every galaxy, every person, is truly his, and is still only the part that came down. Later Hindu texts return to this shape. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna he holds up this whole universe with a single fragment of himself. Different texts, different voices, but the picture rhymes: the divine fully present in the world, and the world not the whole of it. And in a smaller way: whatever you know of anything, a person, a place, a faith, it may be the quarter you've met.
screen: `SUCH IS HIS GREATNESS, AND MORE.` · `PADA: A FOOT, A QUARTER.` · `ALL BEINGS ARE ONE QUARTER.` · `THREE QUARTERS, IMMORTAL IN HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you see often but don't know well, a neighbor, a coworker, a cashier, and picture their face. Then wonder, without guessing details, about the rest of them, the people they love, what they were like as a child, what they're quietly good at, and let them be bigger than the part you've met; if you pray, you can hold them in prayer.

1258.title: the Purusha Sukta
1258.hook: what would you make a world out of? the Purusha Sukta's answer is an offering, with the seasons as its ingredients
1258.howItsDone: Some Hindu households and temples keep the practice of offering into fire, and the Purusha Sukta is among the Vedic hymns recited in worship, where its picture of the first offering is remembered.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Purusha Sukta's proportion: all beings are one quarter of him, and three quarters are immortal in heaven.

What would you make a world out of? Clay, shaped by a potter's hands, is one answer. A spoken word is another. A seed, a shell, a cosmic egg: people have told it more than one way. The Purusha Sukta's answer comes from the fire ritual the hymn itself describes, where offerings are poured into a flame. In this hymn the world comes from an offering, and the ingredients aren't butter and wood. They're spring, summer and autumn.
screen: `CLAY? A WORD? A SEED?` → `THE HYMN'S ANSWER: AN OFFERING.` → `THE INGREDIENTS ARE SEASONS.`

segments.voice: The word is yajna, a sacrifice, an offering poured into fire in Vedic worship. Verse six says that when the gods performed a yajna with the Purusha as the offering, spring was its melted butter, summer its fuel, autumn the offering itself. A fire ritual where the seasons are what's poured in: the year itself, burning as an offering. Verse seven: on the sacred grass they sprinkled him, the one born in the beginning, and the gods and the seers offered with him. From that offering, fully given, came the creatures of the air, the forest and the village. Verse nine turns the hymn back on itself. From that offering were born the verses and the chants, the meters, the sacrificial formulas: the Vedas themselves, the very kind of text the hymn belongs to. A hymn telling where hymns come from. Verse ten adds horses, cattle, goats and sheep. Readers take this offering in different ways. Some traditional readers treat it as a sacred pattern for the fire rituals that followed: what the gods did first, priests repeat. Others read it more inwardly, as the one becoming the many by giving itself away. Either way, in this telling the world isn't built from outside, like a house. It comes from something given, and what comes from it, the songs, the animals, the seasons, carries the mark of that giving.

segments.voice: Notice the season where you are, the light, the air, the temperature on your skin, and bring to mind one thing it has given you lately: a cool morning, a long evening, fruit, rain. On each out-breath, let it go the way something is poured into a fire, not lost but given; if you pray, make the out-breath an offering, and if not, let each breath out be a small giving.

1259.title: the Purusha Sukta
1259.hook: the hymn's eleventh verse is a string of questions: when they divided the Purusha, what was his mouth? the answer has been argued over hard
1259.howItsDone: Hindus read the Purusha Sukta's verse on the four groups in sharply different ways: some as the origin of the varnas, others as a picture of one interdependent body, and reformers have challenged its use to justify caste by birth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Purusha Sukta's great offering: spring as butter, summer as fuel, autumn as the offering, and from it creatures, chants and verses.

When they divided the Purusha, into how many parts did they arrange him? What was his mouth? What were his arms? What are his thighs and feet called? That's the Purusha Sukta's eleventh verse, in paraphrase, nothing but questions, like a teacher quizzing a class. The answer comes in the next verse. It's short, and it has been recited, defended and fought over. You met the caste question on day ninety-five, and in the Gita on day two hundred twenty-two. Today, the verse itself.

segments.voice: Verse twelve answers, in paraphrase: the brahmin, the priest, was his mouth. His arms were made the rajanya, the ruler and warrior. His thighs became the vaishya, the people of trade and farming. From his feet the shudra, the laborer, was born. Four groups, from one body. Notice the wording. The verse doesn't use the word varna, the later word for these social orders, and it doesn't say higher or lower. It names parts of a single person. But readers have heard a ranking in mouth and feet, and that's where the argument begins. Some traditional readers take the verse as the sacred origin of the four varnas. Over time it was also used to defend a ladder fixed by birth, and people outside the four orders altogether were treated as untouchable. Reformers, among them B. R. Ambedkar, attacked that use of the verse directly and fought the system it was used to defend. Other readers, Hindu teachers among them, put the weight elsewhere: all four come from one body, and a body can't live on its mouth alone. Some point to the Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna says the four orders were made according to qualities and actions, and argue that birth was never meant to decide them. These readings don't agree, and this path won't pretend they do. What can be said plainly is what the text says, and what people have done with it. A verse can be held sacred and still need careful hands: hearing the words, and also who has been hurt by how they were used.

1260.title: the Purusha Sukta
1260.hook: "the moon was born from his mind." the Purusha Sukta turns the parts of a body into the sky, the wind and the earth
1260.howItsDone: The Purusha Sukta is recited in Hindu worship and Vedic chanting, and its picture of the world fashioned from the cosmic person's body is echoed in later texts such as the Aitareya Upanishad.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Purusha Sukta's hardest verse: mouth, arms, thighs and feet as four groups, and the honest argument over what that means.

The moon was born from his mind. That's a line from the Purusha Sukta, in paraphrase, and it comes with a whole list. The sun, from his eye. The wind, from his breath. The sky, from his head. Look up some clear night and try reading the sky that way: not as a ceiling, but as a face, a breath, a mind, far bigger than yours and somehow related to yours. The hymn has turned from the people of the world to the world itself, and it draws the map with a body.
screen: `THE MOON, FROM HIS MIND.` → `THE SUN, FROM HIS EYE.` → `A SKY MADE FROM A PERSON.`

segments.voice: Verse thirteen, in Sanskrit, begins chandrama manaso jatah: the moon, born from mind. From his eye, the sun. From his mouth, Indra and Agni, the god of storm and the god of fire. From his breath, Vayu, the wind. Verse fourteen goes on. From his navel, the middle air. From his head, the sky took shape. From his feet, the earth. From his ear, the directions. And so, it says, they fashioned the worlds. Listen to how the pairs fit. Eye and sun: light and seeing. Breath and wind: the same moving air, small and large. Feet and earth: what stands, and what is stood on. Ear and the directions: sound comes from every side. Mind and moon is harder. Some readers hear the moon's waxing and waning as a mind that changes, but the verse only sets the two side by side. Earlier on this path, the Aitareya Upanishad told the same story in reverse: fire became speech and entered the mouth, wind became breath and entered the nose, the sun became sight and entered the eyes, the moon became mind. Together they make a loop. The world comes out of a person, and the world's powers come back to live in a person. This week ran from the Nasadiya's cord and open ending into the Purusha: a thousand heads, the quarter we can see, the great offering, the hard verse, and now the sky. One person, and everything.

segments.voice: Feel the breath at the nostrils and let it be wind for a moment; notice light through closed eyelids and let it be the sun; feel the feet on the floor and let it be the earth; listen for sounds from every side. Then rest the mind and let it be as quiet as the moon, going slowly, body, then world, then body again; if you pray, you can pray there.
